extracted.intended_audience: UIC collection officials, policymakers, legal advisors, and reviewers of unemployment insurance administration
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and procedural criteria for the collection, recovery, write-off, garnishment, Federal Court action, limitation periods, and administrative penalties relating to overpayments under the Unemployment Insurance Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary repayment agreements — factors and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: UIC accepts arrangements that spread repayments over an acceptable period of time; 'What is acceptable is very much left to the discretion of district collection officials.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officials instructed to use 'good judgment on the debtor's ability to repay'. Factors considered in assessing ability to repay: monetary resources; domestic responsibilities and other commitments; amount outstanding; negligence in making earlier repayments; the cause of the overpayment (was fraud involved?). Collection officials are instructed to watch the costs of collection and to keep the period of repayment short relative to the amounts and 'current circumstances'. They are told to avoid instalment arrangements that extend beyond two years and to be aware of statutory limitation periods. Non-compliance (e.g., NSF cheque) triggers telephone contact, then collection letter, then garnishment if the person is working and employer known; Federal Court action may follow where appropriate. If the person later becomes eligible to receive benefits, the agreed weekly amount continues unless the overpayment was caused by fraud. Once collection action has reached issuance of a writ of execution to the sheriff, instalment payments may no longer be authorized by collection officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locating overpayment 'debtors' — methods and confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: A significant proportion of collection officials' time is spent locating ex-claimants and gathering employment/financial information; commercial credit information services may be used when available information is inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officials are instructed not to reveal information in credit reports to the people concerned and not to publicize that UIC uses commercial agencies. Information obtained usually includes current addresses, last known employment and income, and assets assessments. Asset assessments are normally used by regional collection officials when considering Federal Court action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garnishment — prerequisites before initiating
rubrics_metrics.description: Garnishment may be initiated under the Unemployment Insurance Act but is to be used 'with great discretion' when the person is employed and the employer's name and address are known, or against other income and bank accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Garnishment becomes possible only if: the 'debtor' has been clearly notified of the reason for his indebtedness and his right to appeal; all usual and reasonable means of communication (letters, telephone and personal interviews at a minimum) have been exhausted; a minimum of two registered or certified letters of collection have been sent (in addition to the registered/certified letter with the initial demand), with a normal minimum interval of 10 working days between each of these letters; there has been no response to attempts to effect a mutually agreeable settlement; a financial investigation reveals garnishment will not cause undue hardship; and responsible officials consider garnishment necessary because of the debtor's actions/inactions and financial circumstances. When garnishment is commenced, a copy of the third party demand (sent to employer, bank, etc.) must be sent simultaneously to the debtor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garnishment — constraints, fairness and operational limits
rubrics_metrics.description: UIC policies place constraints to protect debtors' circumstances and reputation and to limit the intrusiveness of garnishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constraints include: employers should not be asked to deduct more than 30% of the debtor's salary at any one time; prohibition on garnishing joint bank accounts; limiting garnishment of personal bank accounts to a maximum of one-half of the account. Garnishment is withdrawn if a satisfactory settlement is reached; it ceases if the person loses employment and demands on ex-employers are withdrawn. Officials are instructed to give a further opportunity to repay before initiating garnishment when there has been a gap of several months in written communications. Letters to persons whose wages are being reduced by 30% may state that more satisfactory arrangements can likely be made if the deduction is excessive. The Commission may suggest voluntary repayment to employees (via employers) to avoid the administrative burden of garnishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special procedures for federal employees / Financial Administration Act recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary garnishment procedures do not apply to federal/provincial government employees; special recovery under Financial Administration Act sec.95(1) may be used for federal employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recovery under the Financial Administration Act requires confirmation by the Department of Justice that a debt exists and a request by UIC to Treasury Board. Factors considered before invoking this Act: whether any fault on the part of the employer Department contributed to the debt; whether there will be any 'adverse repercussions' for the Department required to effect recovery; and whether the rate and amount of recovery is reasonable and will not cause undue hardship. UIC procedures require the decision to ask Treasury Board to be supported by detailed reasons for the overpayment, confirmation that the employing Department/agency has been contacted and has no 'justifiable objection', and that a credit report indicates the person will not be caused undue hardship by the contemplated reduction in remuneration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Court action — criteria, process and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Court action (forced sale of debtor's assets) is treated as a 'last-resort' collection method and is appropriate in limited circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In general, Federal Court action may be appropriate where the person is financially able to bear the method, will not agree to repayment arrangements, no other recovery method is available, and the amount involved should be more than $100. Other factors: clear notification to the person of the reason and right to appeal; exhaustion of all usual, reasonable methods of communication; lack of response to attempts to negotiate voluntary settlement; a financial investigation showing Federal Court action will not cause undue hardship; a minimum of two collection letters sent ten days apart. Constraints include immunity for persons aged seventy or more, UIC approval required for sale of real property under execution, and written consent of a very senior official required before attaching personal goods/chattels. Procedure: issuance of certificate to Federal Court (registration/enforcement as a judgment), notifications giving 14 days before certification and further 21 days after judgment during which UIC will accept payments or instalment arrangements (but part payment will not stop proceedings); instalment offers accepted up until sheriff receives writ of execution; once sheriff has writ, repayment offers must be made to sheriff. UIC practice includes renewing judgments and registering them against title until sale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation periods for determination and collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory limitation periods under sec.49(4) and 57(1)/(5) affect all UIC collection methods and determine timeframes for notification and recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination and notification of an overpayment must occur within three years of the overpayment (sec.57(1)). Collection must commence within 36 months of when liability arose, or within 72 months if the Commission considers the overpayment arose because of a false or misleading statement (combined effect: six years, or nine years in case of false/misleading statements, to recover an overpayment). All collection methods except Federal Court action must terminate within these periods; Federal Court action converts a debt to a judgment which is not affected by these limitation periods provided certification occurred before expiry. Voluntary agreements or payments are considered acknowledgement of indebtedness sufficient to bypass limitation periods; when recoupment or garnishment approaches their limitation, officials are instructed to attempt to secure voluntary completion of repayment or an agreement that may include an express waiver of limitation periods. Internal controls should guard against over-zealous attempts to recover before expiration without assessing undue hardship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write-off policies and criteria (amount thresholds, fraud exceptions, and undue hardship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regional officials decide write-offs guided by UIC policies; some write-offs are automatic or rule-based, others discretionary based on uncollectability or undue hardship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specified normal treatments by amount: $1-5 — automatic write-off if the person is not receiving benefits; $6-25 — write-off after one year, minimum of two collection letters and attempt to ascertain employment; $26-50 — write-off after one year normally, or three years if fraud involved, minimum of four collection letters, check at least three sources for location; $51-100 — write-off after one year normally, or three years if fraud involved, provided reasonable collection efforts have been made and failed; $101-200 — write-off after two years normally, or six years if fraud involved, provided reasonable efforts have failed; over $200 — write-off after three years normally, or six years if fraud involved, provided reasonable efforts failed. Discretionary policies allow write-offs if amount is uncollectable or if repayment would result in undue hardship. To qualify for undue hardship write-off, a person should demonstrate incapacity for future work or only limited employment and should have a supporting letter from a medical doctor, a lawyer or a welfare official. UIC auditor may request additional documentation (e.g., communications from welfare agencies, Benefit Control Officers, CPP administrators, financial institutions). Observations indicate regional variation and limited public awareness of write-off discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative penalties — statutory basis, elements, limits and time limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Sec.47(1): Where the Commission becomes aware of facts that in its opinion establish that a claimant or any person on his behalf has knowingly made a false or misleading statement in relation to any claim for benefit, the Commission may impose a penalty not greater than an amount equal to three times his weekly rate of benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The violation contains a factual element (false or misleading statement in relation to a claim for benefit made by the claimant or someone acting on his behalf) and a mental element (knowledge). Only claimants or persons acting on their behalf may be liable under sec.47 (employers may be liable under separate criminal provisions). Administrative penalties are monetary fines only, set by UIC within statutory limit (up to three times weekly rate) and are alternative (not cumulative) to criminal sanctions for the same action. Time limit for imposing administrative penalties is 36 months (sec.47(3)), with the starting point based on date of first or last illegal payment depending on circumstances; criminal sanctions have a longer period (five years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria and guidance for choosing administrative penalties versus criminal prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: UIC guidelines indicate that false or misleading statements normally constitute offences subject to prosecution, and administrative penalties under sec.47 are applicable 'where there are mitigating or extenuating circumstances.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidelines and UIC Manual list mitigating circumstances: claimant's lack of knowledge of some obligations; mistakes resulting from inaccurate information provided by a UIC officer (in which case no sanction may be imposed); state of health (at time of statement or at time of intended prosecution); age (very young or very old); advanced pregnancy; 'good' motives (e.g., to pay large medical expenses). BCO Training Guide adds considerations: avoid prosecution when effect would be more severe than desired (protecting reputation, avoiding loss of present job, not impeding return to field of employment, except in jobs requiring high honesty/integrity). UIC Manual suggests recourse to administrative penalties where witnesses are unavailable or trial costs would be disproportionate, but warns against avoiding prosecution merely to save time/money if guilt can be conclusively proven. Guidelines specify that the amount of the penalty must not exceed the average fines imposed by courts for comparable offences; prosecution may be pursued despite costs if a deterrent effect or correction of critical violation is desired. Choice between sanctions is therefore to be informed by mitigating circumstances, evidentiary considerations, costs, deterrence, and comparability to court fines.
